name: Nitric oxide nasal breathing

lead: Nitric oxide nasal breathing is the belief that air drawn through the nose picks up nitric oxide made in the nasal airways and sinuses, and that this gas helps the lungs absorb oxygen and relaxes blood vessels. Within looksmaxxing it is usually given as one reason to keep the mouth closed and breathe nasally, a habit linked in the community to jaw posture, facial structure and a relaxed look.

Nasal nitric oxide itself is well documented: clinicians measure it to help diagnose primary ciliary dyskinesia, and reviews describe the sinuses as a rich source of the gas. Whether nasal breathing changes oxygen uptake or appearance in healthy people has been proposed in reviews rather than tested in appearance-focused trials.

paras: In practice people practise keeping the lips together and breathing in and out through the nose at rest, while walking and during light exercise, sometimes with mouth taping at night or humming exercises that proponents say increase nasal nitric oxide. Results are described by users as changes in comfort and sleep rather than measured facial change.

Nasal breathing at rest is the normal pattern and carries little risk for most people. Persistent nasal blockage can make it difficult, and clinicians advise assessing chronic obstruction. Practices layered on top, such as taping the mouth shut during sleep, carry their own risks for people with congestion or sleep-breathing problems.

angle.text: People use nasal breathing as a daily habit to support a closed-mouth resting posture, which they associate with a more defined lower face and a rested look. The nitric oxide mechanism is offered as the physiological reason the habit is worthwhile.

lead: Nitric oxide nasal breathing, or the Nasal NO theory, is a community concept holding that breathing through the nose delivers nitric oxide (NO), a gas produced in the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses, to the lungs and that this makes nasal breathing physiologically better than mouth breathing. Looksmaxxing forums fold it into the broader case for nasal breathing and proper tongue and jaw posture.

The appearance chain people draw is: keeping the mouth closed and breathing nasally, which supports a closed-lip resting posture and better sleep and exercise comfort, which they connect with a more defined jawline, better facial development in children and a less fatigued face. The gas itself is real. Reviews describe the sinus lining as continuously generating NO, with concentrations in the sinuses far above those in the nasal cavity, and nasal NO is measured clinically in diagnosing primary ciliary dyskinesia [1][2].

Researchers have proposed that nasally carried NO acts as an airborne messenger that widens pulmonary vessels and improves oxygen uptake. That is a hypothesis in the review literature, and no published trial has tested it as a route to a change in facial appearance.

paras: Nitric oxide is a short-lived signalling molecule that relaxes the smooth muscle in blood vessel walls, widening them and increasing blood flow [3]. In the nose, the gas is produced by the lining of the nasal airways and especially the paranasal sinuses. The theory in looksmaxxing circles takes this physiology and argues that mouth breathing bypasses the source, so that nasal breathing is the way to receive it.
Proponents typically present it as a reason to maintain nasal breathing during exercise and sleep and as supporting evidence for jaw- and tongue-posture practices.

A review of the literature on nitric oxide and the sinuses reports that healthy sinus epithelium expresses inducible nitric oxide synthase and produces large amounts of NO continuously, with sinus levels exceeding nasal cavity levels by one to two orders of magnitude. The same literature proposes that this NO travels to the lungs with each inhalation and induces pulmonary vasodilation, a distal effect on oxygen uptake and cardiac workload.

Other background: Wikipedia notes that nasal breathing yields higher exhaled nitric oxide than mouth breathing [3], and that the nose warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air [4]. Humming has been shown to markedly raise measured nasal nitric oxide, attributed to faster gas exchange between the sinuses and the nose [5]. Humming practices in the community build on this finding.

Clinically, nasal NO is best known as a diagnostic marker. Very low nasal NO is characteristic of primary ciliary dyskinesia, and a European Respiratory Society and American Thoracic Society guideline recommends nasal NO measurement as an adjunct diagnostic test [1][2][6]. Standardised procedures for measuring nasal NO have been published by both societies [7].

Reviewers describe the link between sinus NO and oxygen uptake as a proposed mechanism and the effect on the lungs as distal. Researchers have not published a trial showing that nasal breathing alters facial structure or appearance in adults. A 2023 paper reported by Wikipedia found that acute nasal breathing lowered diastolic blood pressure and increased parasympathetic influence on heart rate variability in young adults [4].

No studies found on nasal nitric oxide breathing as an appearance intervention. Related clinical research covers nasal NO as a diagnostic measurement in primary ciliary dyskinesia [1][6] and the effect of humming on measured nasal NO [5].

The theory is discussed alongside mewing, tongue posture, mouth taping and jaw development. Community members present nasal breathing as a foundation habit, and the nitric oxide mechanism is cited as a physiological reason.
